answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is the final sentence of On the Origin of Species, first edition (London: John Murray, 1859), pp. 489–490 — the last words of the book, closing on “evolved.” The wording above is the 1859 text; from the second edition (1860) onward Darwin inserted “by the Creator” after “breathed,” an edit he later told Joseph Hooker he regretted.

source.heading: The last sentence of the Origin

docMeta.dd: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life
London: John Murray, 24 November 1859 — first edition, 1,250 copies printed
Chapter XIV, “Recapitulation and Conclusion,” pp. 489–490 — the closing sentence of the book
The 2nd (1860) through 6th (1872) editions read “originally breathed by the Creator into a few forms or into one”

source.excerpt: It is interesting to contemplate an entangled bank, clothed with many plants of many kinds, with birds singing on the bushes, with various insects flitting about, and with worms crawling through the damp earth, and to reflect that these elaborately constructed forms, so different from each other, and dependent on each other in so complex a manner, have all been produced by laws acting around us. … Thus, from the war of nature, from famine and death, the most exalted object which we are capable of conceiving, namely, the production of the higher animals, directly follows. There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.
trail: The Wikisource transcription of the 1859 first edition ↗ ends chapter XIV — and the book — with exactly this sentence, with no mention of a Creator.

Wikiquote’s sourced entry for On the Origin of Species ↗ cites it to “1st ed. (1859) pp. 489–90,” notes it is the last paragraph and the only use of the term “evolve” in the original text, and records that Darwin added “by the Creator” in the 2nd (1860) through 6th (1872) editions.

Darwin Online’s bibliographical introduction ↗ dates the first edition to 24 November 1859 (John Murray, 1,250 copies) and the second to 7 January 1860; its editorial introduction to the first edition ↗ quotes the closing sentence in the 1859 form.

Darwin’s own second thoughts survive in his letter to J. D. Hooker of 29 March 1863 ↗: “But I have long regretted that I truckled to public opinion & used Pentateuchal term of creation, by which I really meant ‘appeared’ by some wholly unknown process.”
source.excerptNote: The final paragraph of chapter XIV, abridged in the middle; the closing sentence is given in full, exactly as printed in 1859.

author.name: Charles Darwin
author.heading: Charles Darwin
author.bio: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist, geologist and biologist whose voyage on HMS Beagle supplied the observations behind two decades of private theorising. He published On the Origin of Species in November 1859, setting out descent with modification by natural selection, and spent years revising it through five further editions. He was a careful, anxious writer — and the closing sentence quoted here, the one line in the book that reaches for beauty rather than evidence, is also the one he went back and altered.

misattribution.heading: The line is real — the version you saw may not be
misattribution.intro: Darwin attracts fabricated quotations, but this is not one of them: he wrote every word of it. The problem here is the opposite one — the sentence circulates in shortened, re-punctuated and wrong-edition forms, and people argue about it using text Darwin did not print in 1859.

items.why: Quotefancy ↗ presents it as “There is a grandeur in this view of life, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful are being evolved,” with no source given. Two clauses have been deleted and the tense changed.

Many collections open with “There is a grandeur” — for example Libquotes ↗, citing Great Books of the Western World vol. 49, ch. XV, p. 243. Darwin’s printed text has no “a”: it begins “There is grandeur.”

items.who: Both critics and defenders of Darwin
items.why: The widely circulated “breathed by the Creator into a few forms” wording is genuinely Darwin’s, but it enters only with the second edition ↗ and runs through the sixth of 1872, as Wikiquote records ↗. Quoting it as the 1859 original — in either direction of the argument — misstates what the first edition says.

misattribution.truthLine: The sentence at the top of this page is the 1859 first-edition text, pp. 489–490, exactly as transcribed on Wikisource ↗ — no “a,” no Creator, nothing trimmed.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Darwin had spent the whole book arguing that species are made by struggle, famine and death, and he knew exactly how that would land. So he ended it not with a proof but with a picture: an entangled bank of plants, birds, insects and worms, all of it produced by laws acting around us. The closing sentence is his answer to the charge that his theory drained the world of wonder — the grandeur, he insists, is in the mechanism itself.

The last word of the book is “evolved,” and Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ notes it is the only appearance of the term “evolve” in the original 1859 text. The word we now attach to Darwin’s name shows up once, at the very end, almost in passing.
detailsBody: The Creator crept in afterwards. In the second edition, published on 7 January 1860 ↗, the sentence gained the words “by the Creator” after “breathed,” and it stayed that way through the sixth edition of 1872.

Darwin did not stay comfortable with it. Writing to Joseph Hooker on 29 March 1863 ↗ he said he had “long regretted” that he “truckled to public opinion” and used the “Pentateuchal term of creation,” by which he had really meant “appeared” by some wholly unknown process. He never took the phrase back out of the book.
